content: The approach of lifelong antiretroviral therapy (ART) for all pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV involves administering a triple-drug antiretroviral regimen to all such women, regardless of their CD4 count or clinical stage. This strategy is implemented not only to improve the health of the women themselves but also to prevent vertical transmission of HIV to their children and to provide additional benefits in HIV prevention. This approach was previously referred to as Option B+ in earlier WHO guidelines. The development of these guidelines was co-chaired by Anthony Harries from the International Union Against Tuberculosis and Lung Disease (United Kingdom) and Gottfried Hirnschall from the Department of HIV at the World Health Organization. The Adult Guideline Development Group was co-chaired by Serge Eholié from ANEPA/Treichville Hospital in Côte d’Ivoire and Stefano Vella from Istituto Superiore di Sanità in Italy. The GRADE methodology for evidence review was led by Elie Akl from the American University of Beirut in Lebanon. The Maternal and Child Health Guideline Development Group was co-chaired by Elaine Abrams from the International Center for AIDS Care and Treatment Programs (ICAP) at Columbia University in the USA and Denis Tindyebwa from the African Network for the Care of Children Affected by AIDS in Uganda. The GRADE methodology for this group was led by Joerg Meerpohl from the German Cochrane Centre at the University Medical Center Freiburg in Germany. Acknowledgments were extended to numerous contributors and experts from various institutions worldwide, including representatives from ministries of health, universities, research organizations, and non-governmental organizations. These individuals provided critical input, evidence reviews, and peer reviews to ensure the guidelines were comprehensive and evidence-based. The contributors represented a diverse range of countries, including South Africa, Zambia, Thailand, the USA, France, and many others, reflecting a global effort to address HIV treatment and prevention effectively. The guidelines also benefited from external peer reviewers and modeling work conducted by experts in the field. These efforts were aimed at consolidating the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection, ensuring that the recommendations were grounded in the best available evidence and aligned with global health priorities.
